29374:
Jonah son of Amittai, from Gath-hepher in Galilee, was a prophet of the northern kingdom who correctly foretold Jeroboam II's restoration of Israel's borders. The book bearing his name, however, tells of a very different mission: he was sent to Nineveh, the great city of Assyria, Israel's most feared enemy, and he ran the other way. A storm, a great fish, and a prayer from the deep brought him back; a single short sentence of warning then produced the repentance of the entire city, from king to cattle.

Unlike other prophetic books, Jonah is almost entirely narrative, and its sharpest irony falls on the prophet himself. Pagan sailors and Ninevites respond to God more readily than he does. Jonah's anger is not that his prophecy might fail but that God is exactly as merciful as Israel's creed declared (Exod 34:6). The book ends with God's unanswered question about his compassion for a city of foreigners and animals.

Jesus used 'the sign of Jonah' to speak of his own death and resurrection and to rebuke his generation, saying the men of Nineveh would rise in judgment because they repented at Jonah's preaching. Whether the book records history or is a didactic story is debated, but all readings agree on its theme: the breadth of God's mercy and the narrowness of the human heart.
29375: 2 Kgs 14:25 names him as son of Amittai from Gath-hepher in the days of Jeroboam II. The book narrates his flight (Jonah 1:1-3), the storm (Jonah 1:4-16), the fish (Jonah 1:17), his prayer (Jonah 2:1-9), his preaching (Jonah 3:1-4), Nineveh's repentance (Jonah 3:5-10), and his anger (Jonah 4:1-11). Jesus speaks of the sign of the prophet Jonah, his three days in the belly of the fish, and the Ninevites' repentance (Matt 12:38-41; Matt 16:4; Luke 11:29-32).
29376: The book is read in full at the afternoon service of Yom Kippur as a lesson in repentance and God's readiness to forgive. Some rabbinic interpreters explain Jonah's flight as zeal for Israel, fearing that gentile repentance would shame unrepentant Israel (Mekhilta, Pisha 1).
29378: Jonah is a type of Christ's death, burial and resurrection; the image of Jonah cast up by the fish is one of the most common scenes in early Christian catacomb art. His story also prefigures the gospel going to the gentiles.
29379: The book is historical narrative: Jesus treats Jonah and the Ninevites' repentance as real events alongside the queen of the South, and 2 Kgs 14:25 anchors Jonah in history. The fish is a miracle, not a natural event.
29381: The book is often read as a didactic narrative or satirical parable, probably post-exilic (5th-4th century BC) on grounds of language and theme, using a known prophet as its protagonist to challenge narrow nationalism. Proponents argue that Jesus can cite a story's characters as one cites a parable; critics reply that Jesus' argument assumes real repentance.

29394: Nineveh became Assyria's capital under Sennacherib (c. 700 BC) but was a major city long before. Assyria experienced internal weakness, revolts, plague and a solar eclipse (763 BC) in the first half of the eighth century, which some propose as a background for the city's openness to Jonah's message. The 'king of Nineveh' (Jonah 3:6) is an unusual title, discussed in the dating debate.
29395: Jonah became shorthand for a reluctant prophet and for an unlucky passenger. The book's question about God's compassion for outsiders made it a key text for Christian mission and for Jewish reflection on repentance. The Hebrew 'great fish' was rendered *ketos* (sea monster) in Greek (Matt 12:40), later popularly 'whale'. Augustine and Jerome corresponded over Jerome's translation of the plant as ivy rather than gourd, a change that reportedly caused an uproar in a North African congregation.

29562: Sennacherib ruled Assyria from 705 to 681 BC and rebuilt Nineveh as a magnificent capital. In 701 BC he crushed a western rebellion, devastating Judah and besieging Lachish, but did not take Jerusalem. The Bible attributes his withdrawal to the angel of the LORD; his own annals claim victory and tribute but notably do not claim Jerusalem's capture. He was murdered by his sons twenty years later.
